Need to search first.I've put together verse-by-verse notes for 2 Samuel 18 from the pages I could read. The search and fetch tools hit their usage limits partway through, so I couldn't open several sources you listed: netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org, lcms.org, 1517.org, ag.org, seedbed.com, catholic.com, oca.org and samstorms.org. As a result:

- There are no modern-scholarship notes from the NET Bible or Bible Odyssey.
- There are no Lutheran, Assemblies of God (Pentecostal) or Orthodox entries.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

Many notes come from search-result excerpts of the pages rather than the full pages. Bible Hub and StudyLight pages collect several commentators, so I name the commentator wherever the page does.

---

## 2 Samuel 18: notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik says David knew exactly how to organise his army, and split it into three divisions under Joab, Abishai and Ittai. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- The Expositor's Bible notes that Josephus puts David's force at 4,000. Phrases like "captains of thousands" (v. 1), "ten thousand of us" (v. 3) and "by thousands" (v. 4) suggest it was many thousands. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-samuel-18.html
- Constable and Precept Austin both point out that David is called "the king" five times in vv. 1–5. This leaves no doubt who the real ruler is. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-18.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-18-commentary

**v. 2**
- Gill says David wanted to go out partly to encourage the troops and share their danger, but mainly to save Absalom's life if he could. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html
- Matthew Henry contrasts the two kings. Absalom's false friend talked him into going to battle, which fed his pride. David's true friends kept him back, remembering Ahithophel's plan to kill only the king. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm

**v. 3**
- Text note: Ellicott, Clarke and the Cambridge Bible say the Hebrew literally reads "now there are ten thousand like us." Changing one letter gives "you are worth ten thousand of us," which follows the Greek (Septuagint) and Latin (Vulgate). The Pulpit Commentary adds that the Syriac agrees with the Hebrew. Ewald worked out from "half of us" and "ten thousand" that the army was about 20,000. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-3.html
- Gill thinks David's "help from the city" could mean sending supplies or reinforcements. He prefers the reading of the Targum (an Aramaic paraphrase) and Jewish commentators: David would help by praying for them. Poole calls Absalom's choice to lead in person a "Divine infatuation" that ruined him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-3.htm
- The Geneva Bible note says a good ruler is so dear to his people that they would rather die than see him harmed. Matthew Henry says subjects should value their princes like this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-3.html
- Precept Austin lists three reasons the people gave: David is the enemy's main target, he is worth more than 10,000 soldiers, and he can help from Mahanaim. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-18-commentary
- Christ-centred applications: a Pulpit Commentary homily (G. Wood) applies the verse to Christ, "chiefest among ten thousand." Guzik makes the people's devotion a model of believers' devotion to King Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-18.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 4**
- The Pulpit Commentary says David gave in because it would steady his men to know an experienced leader was held in reserve to help any division in trouble. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-18.html
- Guzik says the troops willingly took on danger for their king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 5**
- Wesley (Methodist) says "deal gently" means: take him prisoner, don't kill him. He gives four reasons for the request: David's indulgence of his children, his awareness that his own sins caused the rebellion, Absalom's youth, and David's wish that Absalom not die in his sin without time to repent. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xi.xix.ii.html
- Constable suggests David asked for gentleness because God had been gentle with David's own sins. He also quotes a writer who says David acted as a father, not a king, treating treason like a family quarrel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-18.html
- Precept Austin says losing Absalom was the third part of the "fourfold" discipline David had pronounced on himself (2 Sam 12:6). The four were: the baby son, Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-18-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik says David's men fought "against Israel" because Israel had been won over by Absalom's charm and power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 7**
- Gill says the 20,000 dead were all on Absalom's side and include those killed in the chase. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html
- Guzik credits the win mainly to David's experienced commanders. He quotes Baldwin: David chose ground where individual skill counted for more than numbers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 8**
- Guzik takes "the forest devoured" to mean God fought for David in unusual ways. He notes the usual view (pits and swamps) and that the Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic versions say wild beasts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- Matthew Henry says the rebels' escape into the woods destroyed them. God fought for David, yet also against him, because the dead were his own subjects. He notes that Rome allowed no victory parade for a civil war. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm
- Constable says it isn't clear how the forest did this, but it suggests the LORD helped David. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-18.html

**v. 9**
- **Hair or head?**
  - Ellicott and Clarke say the text doesn't say he hung by his hair. That idea seems to come from Josephus, though Ellicott allows the hair may have helped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-9.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-9.html
  - Coffman says the text doesn't support Josephus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-9.html
  - Barnes, Benson and Poole think his hair probably was the cause, making his pride the tool of his ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-9.htm
  - Guzik says he was "literally caught by his own hair," while noting Clarke's caution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
  - Precept Austin quotes Walton: the text says head, not hair. The royal mule abandoning the would-be king is full of symbolism. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-18-commentary
- Gill says riding mules was usual for great men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html
- Bible Hub's study notes link hanging on a tree to Deut 21:23 (being under God's curse), which points to Christ bearing the curse (Gal 3:13). https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/18-9.htm
- Guzik also quotes a Jewish legend (Ginzberg) that Absalom saw hell opening below him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**vv. 10–13**
- Guzik says the soldier held back out of loyalty to David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- Gill (v. 12) says the soldiers were told both to hold back themselves and to stop others. On v. 13, he says killing Absalom would have meant betraying the king and acting against the man's own conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html

**v. 14**
- Gill thinks the "darts" may have been rods or iron-tipped staffs. He reads "heart" as the middle of the body, since Absalom was still alive afterwards. Guzik says the same about "heart." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- **Was Joab right?** This is the main point where teachers differ, though not along denominational lines.
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel): Joab was "correct" but not "right." The outcome was better for Israel, but he disobeyed God's appointed authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
  - Clarke, quoted by Guzik: Absalom deserved death, but this was "base and disloyal, and a cowardly murder." Guzik adds that Joab was later held to account (1 Kings 2:5–6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
  - Matthew Henry: he doesn't know that Joab can be justified, yet Joab served king and country by overruling a too-indulgent father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm
  - Gill (Baptist): Joab disobeyed but provided for the nation and the king's safety. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html
  - Cambridge Bible: killing Absalom was the fastest way to end the revolt, and Joab probably settled a personal grudge at the same time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-15.htm

**v. 15**
- An exegetical note on Bible Hub reads it this way: while Absalom was still alive, ten armour-bearers surrounded him and finished him off. That explains why three spears didn't kill him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-15.htm
- Wesley says much the same: the darts didn't kill him, so they struck again. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xi.xix.ii.html
- Gill reports a Jewish "measure for measure" reading:
  - hanged by the hair he was proud of;
  - ten young men for the ten concubines he took;
  - three darts for the three "hearts" he stole: his father's, the Sanhedrin's and Israel's.
  Guzik also quotes the concubines link. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 17**
- Benson and Poole say the stone heap was a lasting mark of his shame. It echoes Achan and the kings of Ai and the Amorites (Josh 7:26; 8:29; 10:27), and it amounted to the stoning a rebellious son deserved (Deut 21:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-17.htm
- Gill agrees but adds it might also have been an honour, since heaps of stones marked graves of the great. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-17.htm
- Clarke says cairns were used for heroes and traitors alike. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-17.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Matthew Henry note travellers' reports that passers-by threw stones on the heap and cursed rebellious sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-17.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-17.html
- Guzik says Joab made sure Absalom's grave would not become a rallying point for rebels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- Bible Hub's notes link the scattering of the troops to Zech 13:7 and Lev 26:17. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/18-17.htm

**v. 18**
- **"I have no son"** (compare 14:27, which names three sons):
  - Guzik and Constable: the sons probably died young. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-17.html
  - Matthew Henry: God took them, and "justly is a rebellious son written childless." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm
  - Bible.org: Absalom built the pillar at a time when he had no sons. https://bible.org/question/2-sam-1427-bible-says-absalom-had-sons-and-1818-absolom-says-i-have-no-son-who-will-carry-m
  - Coffman, citing Payne: he may have built it when his sons died. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-17.html
- Guzik, Matthew Henry and Wesley see the pillar as self-promotion. A rough heap of stones became his real memorial, and his name lives on in disgrace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm ; https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xi.xix.ii.html
- Gill says "Absalom's place" is literally his "hand," meaning the work of his hand, an obelisk. The Latin Vulgate has *Manus Absalom* ("Absalom's hand"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html ; https://www.newadvent.org/bible/2sa018.htm
- Constable explains that a son normally put up his famous father's memorial. The King's Valley is the Kidron, and the 52-foot "Tomb of Absalom" there now dates from the early first century AD, so it is not this pillar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/18-18.html

**vv. 19–23**
- Guzik says Joab wanted to spare Ahimaaz from carrying bad news. Gill says Joab respected Ahimaaz as a priest's son and knew the news would not win him the king's favour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-18.html
- A sermon-style exposition on Bible Hub's 18:18 page reads Ahimaaz, Joab and the Cushite as three kinds of people too wrapped up in themselves to feel David's grief:
  - Ahimaaz is loyal but young and excited, and can't put himself in the father's place. The word for "tidings" always means good news.
  - Joab assumes nobody works without a reward (v. 22).
  - The Cushite was probably an Ethiopian slave, chosen because nobody would miss him if David lashed out.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm
- Matthew Henry suggests two motives for Ahimaaz. He may have wanted to show off his speed by taking the longer route and still winning. Or he may have wanted, out of kindness, to soften the blow by preparing David before the Cushite arrived. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm

**v. 24**
- Wesley says city gates were large and doubled, an outer and an inner one, and David sat between them to hear news. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xi.xix.ii.html
- The same Bible Hub exposition says the change of scene to Mahanaim builds the suspense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm

**vv. 25–27**
- The exposition notes that David reasoned a man running alone must be a messenger. A second runner suggested something more had happened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm

**v. 28**
- The same exposition says Ahimaaz shows more devotion than David: he gives God the credit, while David shows no thanks to God or his men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm

**v. 29**
- Ellicott calls the reply a skilful but untruthful dodge, and says Ahimaaz had been "trained to untruthfulness" in David's spy service. The Cambridge Bible agrees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-29.htm
- Gill says that though Ahimaaz was a good man, "he cannot be excused from lying." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-29.htm
- Text note: Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible suggest "the king's servant" may have slipped in from a margin note. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-29.htm
- Gill notes the Hebrew literally asks "Is there peace to the young man?" The Cambridge Bible quotes a writer who says calling him "the youth" treats his youth as excuse enough. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-29.htm
- Guzik says Ahimaaz was the better runner but the worse messenger, because he didn't know his message. He also faults David for caring more about his son than the nation, while seeing in the question a picture of God's love for his children. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/

**v. 30**
- The Bible Hub exposition calls the brush-off "a cool reception, unworthy of David." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm

**vv. 31–32**
- Ellicott says the Cushite answers plainly but politely that Absalom is dead. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/18-32.htm
- Matthew Henry says he broke the news so tactfully that he could not be blamed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_018.cfm
- Bible Hub's notes say the polite blessing carries a solemn verdict: Absalom's fate becomes the pattern for every revolt against the Lord's anointed (Ps 2). https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/18-32.htm

**v. 33**
- Guzik and Gill say "shaken" suggests violent trembling. Gill adds that David hurried to the watchtower room so he could grieve in private. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-33.htm
- **Why did he grieve this way?** Again the teachers differ:
  - Wesley and Gill both mention the view that David grieved over Absalom's eternal fate, since he died in his sins. Both lean instead to strong natural feeling, which Wesley calls speaking "unadvisedly." https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.ii.xi.xix.ii.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-33.htm
  - Matthew Henry blames David for doting on a graceless son and for quarrelling with God's justice and the nation's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-33.htm
  - A further note on the same Bible Hub page adds that David's anger at Joab for ignoring his order kept him from seeing the justice of God in the death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-33.htm
  - Guzik, using G. Campbell Morgan: David saw his own sins and his indulgent parenting magnified in Absalom, so parents must first train themselves in godliness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/ ; https://enduringword.com/anguish-father/
  - The Bible Hub exposition says grief is not forbidden, but David's blinded him to his duties and his blessings. It was the bitter fruit of his own sin, yet it also shows a father's self-giving love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/18-18.htm
- B. Dale's sermon counts "my son" five times and "Absalom" three times. It quotes Kirkpatrick: "Would God I had died for thee" was also David admitting that he deserved the punishment. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/dale/david's_lament_over_absalom.htm
- Guzik draws a Christ-centred point: what David could not do, God did by dying in rebels' place. He quotes Chuck Smith: we hear in David "the cry of God" for his lost children. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-18/
- In a follow-up devotional, Guzik says David lost perspective and let his feelings rule him (the story continues into ch. 19). https://enduringword.com/given-over-to-grief/

---

## Catholic readings (Church Fathers on newadvent.org)
- **Augustine, on Psalm 3:** he gives "Absalom" as "father's peace." David stayed at peace with his son even in the war, as his grief shows, and Absalom is compared with Judas. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
- **Augustine, Letter 185:** David gave orders to spare Absalom so he could forgive him if he repented. Peace for David's house came only through Absalom's death, so David could only weep and take comfort in the peace. Augustine compares this to the Church grieving over those who are lost. Thomas Aquinas repeats the point. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102185.htm ; https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3010.htm
- **Ambrose, On Repentance II.11:** David's cry shows the endless grief over a sinner who died without repenting. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34062.htm
- **Dale's sermon** quotes Augustine as saying Absalom grieved his father more by his death than by his life. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/dale/david's_lament_over_absalom.htm

## How the traditions compare
The teachers I could read (Wesley for Methodists; Gill for Baptists; Matthew Henry; Guzik and Smith of Calvary Chapel, which I've put under your charismatic heading) agree on the main lines. Absalom's death was God's judgment on pride and rebellion, and David's grief came partly from his own sin and indulgence. They differ in degree on three points:
- whether Joab can be excused (v. 14);
- whether David's cry was proper fatherly love or excessive passion (v. 33);
- how far to read Christ into the text (vv. 3 and 33).

I found no split along denominational lines.
